overview:
Japan is an island country off the east coast of Asia, a long curve of thousands of islands in the Pacific Ocean. Four main islands, Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu, hold most of its land and people, with the tropical Okinawa islands trailing far to the south. The country covers about 378,000 km², slightly smaller than California, and about 124 million people live there, packed onto the coastal plains because mountains cover about three-quarters of the land.

Tokyo, the capital, is the center of the largest metropolitan area on Earth, home to about 37 million people, yet its trains run on time to the second and its streets are famously clean. Japanese is the language, written with thousands of characters plus two phonetic alphabets. Japan is a constitutional monarchy: the emperor is a ceremonial head of state from the world's oldest royal family, while an elected parliament and prime minister govern.

Japan is known for blending ancient traditions such as tea ceremonies and temples with cutting-edge robots, bullet trains, video games and anime.
landAndNature:
Japan sits where four plates of the Earth's crust meet, so it has about 110 active volcanoes and thousands of earthquakes a year. Mount Fuji, a near-perfect snow-capped cone of about 3,776 meters, is the highest and most beloved peak. In 2011 a huge earthquake and tsunami struck the northeast coast, killing about 20,000 people. Hot springs called onsen bubble up everywhere, and even wild snow monkeys soak in them in winter.

Climate ranges from snowy Hokkaido, one of the snowiest places on Earth, to subtropical Okinawa. Spring brings the pink wave of cherry blossoms that sweeps north across the country, and autumn turns the maple forests red. Wildlife includes the Japanese macaque, sika deer, the huge Japanese giant salamander, red-crowned cranes and brown bears in Hokkaido.
peopleAndCulture:
Japanese culture prizes politeness, harmony and attention to detail. People bow in greeting, remove shoes indoors, and take care to keep public places spotless. Shinto shrines with red gates and Buddhist temples stand in every town, and matsuri festivals fill the streets with floats, drums and fireworks. Families gather in spring for hanami picnics under the cherry blossoms.

Food is an art: sushi, ramen, tempura, and bento lunch boxes arranged like pictures. Baseball is the most popular sport, and sumo wrestling, judo and karate are traditional ones. Japan invented manga comics, anime, karaoke, instant noodles and emoji, and its video games and robots are known worldwide. Children fold origami cranes, and traditional arts like calligraphy, flower arranging and the tea ceremony are still taught.
history:
The Jōmon people made some of the world's oldest pottery in Japan more than 14,000 years ago. Rice farming, writing and Buddhism arrived from China and Korea, and by the 700s emperors ruled from Nara and then Kyoto. From 1192 military lords called shoguns held real power, with samurai warriors serving them; Mongol invasions in the 1200s were defeated with help from typhoons. The Tokugawa shoguns closed Japan to most of the world for 250 years.

After American ships forced the country open in 1853, the Meiji Restoration of 1868 modernized Japan at astonishing speed. It built an empire, invaded China and attacked the United States at Pearl Harbor in 1941. World War II ended after atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, killing well over 100,000 people. Japan adopted a peaceful constitution in 1947, rebuilt into the world's second-largest economy by the 1970s, and remains a leading technological nation.
funFacts: Japan has about 5 million vending machines, roughly one for every 25 people, selling everything from hot coffee to umbrellas.
The world's oldest company, Kongō Gumi, built temples in Japan continuously from 578 AD until 2006.
Shinkansen bullet trains have carried billions of passengers since 1964 without a single fatal accident caused by derailment or collision.
Japan's emperors trace their line back more than 1,500 years, the oldest continuous monarchy in the world.
Farmers in Japan grow square watermelons in glass boxes so they stack neatly in refrigerators.
A 2023 recount found Japan has 14,125 islands, more than double the number previously listed.
